title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can produce argumentative essays that are comparable to, or better than, essays written by students. The authors focus on a practical education-related concern: if generative AI can write high-quality essays, then traditional homework and essay grading may need to change. They also examine whether AI-generated writing has distinctive linguistic properties compared with human student writing.

The study compares 90 human-written argumentative essays from an essay-feedback forum used by German high-school students with essays generated by ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt asking for an essay of about 200 words on the same topic. Teachers at secondary schools participated as expert raters after a short online training session; they evaluated anonymized essays on seven criteria including topic completeness, logic, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs. The authors also conducted a computational linguistic analysis of lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modality, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The results show that both ChatGPT versions were rated higher than the human-written essays on all major essay-quality criteria, with ChatGPT-4 outperforming ChatGPT-3. The AI texts were structurally more rigid and differed linguistically from student writing: they used more nominalizations and more complex sentence structures, while students used more modals and epistemic markers. The authors conclude that generative AI can already perform strongly on this kind of school writing task and argue that educators should adapt homework and writing instruction accordingly. They also note that hallucinations were not a major issue for this argumentative-essay task, though they caution that subtle errors may have been missed and that the models are fast-changing targets.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot interface based on GPT-family models, used to generate and interact with text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate argumentative student essays from 90 topics via zero-shot prompts, compared against human-written essays and across ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 outputs for essay quality and linguistic characteristics.

findings.finding_summary: In a large-scale essay evaluation with 111 teachers and 658 ratings across 270 essays, ChatGPT-generated essays were rated significantly higher than human-written essays on all seven rubric criteria. Mean overall ratings were 4.36 for ChatGPT-3 and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4 versus 3.69 for human essays; reported effects for human vs. ChatGPT-3 ranged from d=0.52 to 1.15 and for human vs. ChatGPT-4 from d=0.88 to 1.43.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated essay quality on seven criteria (topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, language constructs) and overall score
findings.sample_size: n=270 essays rated by 111 teachers; 658 ratings

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT essays showed distinct linguistic patterns relative to human essays: they had higher sentence complexity and nominalizations, but also differed in modal use, epistemic markers, and discourse markers. The paper reports significant differences in most linguistic markers, with no significant difference for sentence complexity (depth) between humans and ChatGPT-3, and no significant difference for discourse markers between humans and ChatGPT-3.
findings.measure: Computational linguistic markers (lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalizations, modals, epistemic markers, discourse markers)

findings.finding_summary: The authors report that hallucinations were not a major problem in this argumentative essay setting because the tasks relied on general argumentation rather than factual correctness. They also caution that subtle hallucinations may have been missed and note some low ratings for criteria related to factual correctness.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings plus qualitative discussion of factual correctness/hallucination risk

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single observational comparative study with teacher ratings and computational linguistic analysis, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The design is systematic and statistically rigorous, but it remains correlational/benchmark-style evidence rather than intervention evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are large in magnitude for essay quality (many effects well above d=0.20, often medium-to-large or larger). The paper suggests substantial educational implications for homework and writing instruction, indicating high potential impact.
